title: A loop goes somewhere.
teaser: A leaf vein helps Little see how a loop becomes a journey.
question: How does an inchworm turn a loop into a step?
idea: An inchworm is a geometer moth caterpillar. Its front legs grip as its rear moves forward, raising a loop. Then its rear prolegs grip while its front reaches ahead. A long middle without walking legs makes this alternating movement especially clear.

curiosity.intro: Choose a question. Look for a clue in the picture, then test your first idea against the explanation.
curiosity.carryForward: Follow the grips through the story. Use a leaf vein as evidence, work out a pretend journey, and explain a discovery in your own words.

questions.question: Why does the middle rise into a loop?
questions.notice: Find the head at the right. Follow the body back to the rear feet. Where is there empty space underneath?
questions.say: The front legs hold the leaf while the rear comes closer. The long middle bends upward into a loop. Inchworms have jointed legs near the head and fleshy gripping parts called prolegs near the rear, with a long gap between. They do not walk on a row of legs along that middle.
questions.try: Draw a long curved line with its two ends close together. Imagine the front end stays in one place as the rear comes closer. Which part must bend?

questions.question: What holds on while the head reaches?
questions.notice: The front is lifted. Follow the body to the far left. Which feet still touch the leaf?
questions.say: Now the rear prolegs anchor the body: they hold it in place. The front reaches ahead as the middle straightens. When the front legs grip again, the rear can catch up. The two ends take turns holding on. That repeating sequence carries the caterpillar across a leaf.
questions.try: Look at the rear grip. What might happen if it slipped while the front was still reaching? Use a detail from the picture to explain.

questions.question: How could a leaf vein show it moved?
questions.notice: Compare the two leaf sketches. Each dot records the head. Find the same Y-shaped vein fork in both. What changed?
questions.say: A bent body alone does not tell us how far the animal traveled. The first head mark is before the fork; the later mark is beyond it. The fork is a reference point, a place to compare positions against. Those changed positions are evidence for movement. They do not tell us its speed without times.
questions.try: Draw a Y and put a dot before it. Draw the same Y again with a dot beyond it. Explain how the two drawings support the idea that the head moved.

questions.question: Will this caterpillar always crawl?
questions.notice: Find three life stages in the notebook. How does the last shape differ from the first?
questions.say: An inchworm is a caterpillar, the young stage of a geometer moth. It grows, becomes a pupa, then changes into a moth. This big change in body form is metamorphosis. It takes time; this scene imagines a later stage. A moth has six jointed legs. The caterpillar's fleshy prolegs do not remain.
questions.try: Follow the notebook arrows: caterpillar, pupa, moth. Name one body feature that changes. What extra observation would help you learn how long the change takes?

plates.title: A traveling arch
plates.alt: An enlarged green inchworm arches over a sunlit leaf, head at right and rear grips at left. Big and Little watch from the garden path; a dew drop rests below.
plates.caption: An imagined close view of a leaf journey. The caterpillar is enlarged; the picture is not a ruler.

plates.title: The rear catches up
plates.alt: The inchworm's front legs hold near a leaf vein at right. Its legless middle forms an arch; an orange arrow near the rear points toward the front.
plates.caption: Front grips; rear comes closer. Notice the long legless middle rather than counting the partly hidden feet.

plates.title: A grip, then a reach
plates.alt: The rear prolegs grip a leaf at left while the inchworm's long body straightens and its head reaches right. The little front legs are lifted; an orange arrow points ahead.
plates.caption: Rear grips; front reaches. This simplified still picture shows one moment in a repeating movement.

plates.title: The leaf keeps a clue
plates.alt: Big and Little study a living leaf beside a notebook. In two sketches of the same vein fork, the head-position dot is first before the fork and later beyond it.
plates.caption: Two imagined observations of the same leaf. Compare the head marks against the same fork.

plates.title: A pretend leaf journey
plates.alt: Little holds a pencil above a notebook leaf drawing with a winding orange route and pencil dots. Big watches beside Little; an inchworm loops along a nearby leafy twig.
plates.caption: A drawing model for a journey. Use the invented table distances, not the picture's size or dot spacing.

plates.title: A later shape
plates.alt: A gray-brown geometer moth rests on a twig at dusk. Beside Big and Little, a notebook shows caterpillar, pupa and moth sketches joined by orange arrows.
plates.caption: An imagined later life stage. The notebook skips time; this change does not happen during one evening.

reading.title: A loop goes somewhere
reading.coverText: A green arch rises on a leaf. A head reaches. Follow the tiny grips that carry one inchworm across.
reading.parentNote: About 15 minutes. Support pronunciation when useful, then let Leo revisit a picture and explain the mechanism. Evidence and inference are deliberately a small step beyond a basic sequence retell. All kid-facing directions address Leo; the same story appears on screen, Letter and foldable.

beats.title: The arch begins
beats.passage: Little spots a green arch on the leaf. “A tiny bridge!” The arch flattens, and a small head reaches past a vein. Big watches from the path. Bending is how this caterpillar starts a trip across the same leaf vein.
beats.prompt: Which parts are touching the leaf right now?
beats.wink: Bridges this small skip the toll.

beats.title: The rear catches up
beats.passage: Front grips hold the leaf. The rear slides closer and the long middle lifts into a tall loop. Soft grips near the rear are prolegs — fleshy holders, not jointed walking legs. “No walking legs under that middle,” Little says.
beats.prompt: Which end stays put while the loop rises?
beats.wink: Middle of the road: no feet on duty.

beats.title: Hold, then reach
beats.passage: The prolegs anchor the rear: they hold it in place. The front stretches ahead as the body straightens. When the front grips again, the rear can follow. One end holds; the other moves. Loop by loop, the leaf gets shorter.
beats.prompt: What might go wrong if the rear slipped mid-reach?
beats.wink: Hold still. Then steal a step.

beats.title: A clue on the leaf
beats.passage: Little draws the head before a vein fork, then after it on the same leaf vein. The two marks are evidence — clues that can support an idea. “It passed the fork!” That idea is an inference: an idea drawn from evidence.
beats.prompt: Why is a moved head a stronger clue than a bent body alone?

beats.title: A pretend leaf route
beats.passage: “Does every loop go one inch?” Little asks. The name sounds like a ruler, but real steps vary. So Little invents a pretend route with made-up distances. A model can answer a math question without turning the picture into a measuring stick.
beats.prompt: What would you need to measure a real leaf trip?

beats.title: A later shape
beats.passage: Little imagines later chapters. The caterpillar becomes a pupa, then a moth. That change of body form is metamorphosis, and it takes time. “A new shape after all those loops,” Little grins.
beats.prompt: Which stage sits between caterpillar and moth?

questions: What evidence shows the head traveled rather than only bending in place? Why compare it with the same vein fork?
During the reach, what anchors the rear? Predict what could happen if that grip slipped, and explain why.
reading.coverWink: Psst — the leaf is the map.

math.title: How much leaf is left?
math.intro: Imagine a 32-millimeter route on a leaf. A pretend inchworm walks 12 mm, then 9 mm. A millimeter is a tiny length unit; mm is the short name. Use the table. Show your thinking.
math.printNote: Use the table numbers. The picture is not a ruler.

tasks.label: ADD TWO PARTS
tasks.prompt: Walk 12 mm, then 9 mm. How far in all?
tasks.hint: Add 12 and 9. You can make a ten first if that helps.

tasks.label: HOW MUCH IS LEFT
tasks.prompt: Route is 32 mm. After 12 mm and 9 mm, how much is left? Show both steps.
tasks.hint: First add 12 and 9. Then take that sum away from 32.

tasks.label: A LONGER ROUTE
tasks.prompt: Add 8 mm to the 32 mm route. After a 21 mm walk, how much is left?
tasks.hint: Make the new whole first (32 + 8). Then subtract 21.

tasks.label: THREE LITTLE WALKS
tasks.prompt: A trip goes 7 mm, then 6 mm, then 5 mm. How far in all?
tasks.hint: Add any two first, then add the last number.

tasks.label: COMPARE TWO TRIPS
tasks.prompt: Trip A: 12+9 mm. Trip B: 7+6+5 mm. Which is longer, and by how much?
tasks.hint: Find each total. Subtract the smaller total from the bigger one.
tasks.answer: The first trip is longer by 3 mm. 21 − 18 = 3.

tasks.label: SHARE THE LEFT-OVER
tasks.prompt: 11 mm left. Two friends share it as evenly as they can. How much each, and how much left over?
tasks.hint: How many groups of 2 fit in 11? What is left?
tasks.answer: 5 mm each, with 1 mm left over.

math.extension: Keep using mm. Show each step.
math.parentNote: About 15 minutes. Use a bar model or number-line hops. Read parentheses as 'do this part first'; two separate number sentences are equally useful. The table and route are invented, not measured observations, species speeds, or loop lengths. The final explanation checks that Leo connects the two results: 11 + 8 = 19.

writing.title: Explain a tiny grip.
writing.intro: Choose a scene. Write two linked sentences: one observation, then an explanation using because. Draw a detail that supports your idea.
writing.draw: Draw the detail you noticed. Add an arrow to show movement or a dot to show position.

frames.hint: What happens when the rear gets closer to the gripping front?
What keeps the body in place while the front reaches?

frames.start: I infer that it moved because
frames.hint: Compare the head with the same vein fork in both sketches.

writing.check: Reread your words. Does the detail support your explanation? Check the first capital and each ending mark.
writing.parentNote: About 15 minutes. Welcome Leo's own phrasing, invented spelling, drawing, speech or dictation in adult support. Keep the observation distinct from the inference without demanding formal terms. If needed, scribe his words exactly. The printed prompts stay addressed to Leo.

answers.label: Math · 1
answers.text: 21 mm traveled: 12 + 9 = 21. A bridge-through-ten strategy is 12 + 8 + 1.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: 11 mm left. First combine the traveled stretches: 12 + 9 = 21. Then subtract from the whole: 32 − 21 = 11. Accept two number sentences or a labeled bar model.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: 19 mm left: 32 + 8 = 40 mm; 40 − 21 = 19 mm. Or add 8 to the earlier remainder: 11 + 8 = 19. The traveled distance stays 21 mm.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: The head was before the fork and later beyond it. The same body part changed position beside the same reference point. An arch alone shows shape, not travel. Times would be needed to find speed.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Rear prolegs anchor the body. If they slip before the front grips, the body could slide. Accept a reasoned prediction; it need not claim the animal must fall.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Look for observation plus explanation: The front feet are lifted. The rear prolegs hold because the front cannot grip yet. Or: The head mark passed the fork, so I infer movement. Drawing or dictation can preserve this reasoning.

parentGuidance: These are imagined, enlarged scenes, not an identified species or exact leg-count diagrams. Inchworms are geometer moth caterpillars, not earthworms. They generally have three pairs of jointed front legs and two or three pairs of rear prolegs, with a long legless middle; details vary. Tiny hooks on prolegs help grip. Front legs anchor during looping; rear prolegs anchor during extension. Caterpillar, pupa and moth are stages separated by time; timing varies. The pictured winged moth is a possible adult form, though some females have reduced or absent wings. Most inchworms eat plant material, often leaves. The name suggests measuring, not exactly one-inch steps. Compare the same head against the same vein; position evidence alone gives no speed. All millimeter distances are invented and independent of loop count or art scale. Observe a leaf in place if desired; handling or raising animals is unnecessary. Support pronunciation, invented spelling or dictation as useful. Keep adult guidance in this key or collapsed details.
